MathDraw Studio

Mathematical Foundations, Algorithms, Software Architecture, Validation, and Use of Image-to-Equation Conversion

Technical report for MathDraw Studio v0.2.1

2 August 2026

Abstract

MathDraw Studio converts a raster image into a finite mathematical model and renders that model back into an image. The central design decision is that no single representation is uniformly suitable for drawings, silhouettes, and photographs. The implemented system therefore provides three complementary models: a hybrid vector model composed of line, circle, ellipse-capable, and cubic Bezier primitives; a Fourier contour model for closed planar curves; and an orthonormal two-dimensional discrete cosine transform model for full-tone images. This report develops the mathematical basis of each representation, explains the complete processing pipeline, documents the software implementation as delivered in version 0.2.1, analyzes exactness and approximation, and records validation, failure modes, and extension paths. The account is code-concordant: where an architectural intention or earlier prose differs from the executable source, the behavior of the source and tests is stated explicitly.

1. Executive summary

MathDraw Studio addresses a question that is simple to state and mathematically subtle: given an arbitrary image, what equations can reproduce it? A raster image is already a finite mathematical object, namely a rectangular array of samples. It can therefore be represented exactly by many finite bases. What is not generally available is a short, unique, semantically meaningful closed-form equation for every possible image. A photograph of a peacock, a hand-drawn logo, a geometric diagram, and a food photograph contain different kinds of structure. Treating them with one universal curve-fitting rule would either discard important information or produce an equation set so large that it ceases to be useful.

The project resolves this by separating representation choice from equation generation. Three modes are provided.

  1. Hybrid vector mode is intended for drawings, diagrams, lettering, logos, and other images dominated by boundaries and sparse regions. Straight structures are detected by a probabilistic Hough procedure; circular structures may be detected by a circular Hough procedure; residual foreground regions are traced as contour hierarchies, simplified, and stored as piecewise cubic Bezier paths.
  2. Fourier contour mode models each closed boundary as a finite complex Fourier series. Low-frequency harmonics reproduce the global shape, while additional harmonics restore progressively finer detail.
  3. DCT image mode models each luminance or color channel on a selected grid by an orthonormal two-dimensional discrete cosine basis. Retaining all coefficients gives an exact reconstruction of that selected grid up to floating-point arithmetic and final integer rounding. Retaining only the largest coefficients gives a compressed approximation.

The distinction between exactness of the represented grid and fidelity to the original file is fundamental. If a 2000 by 1100 RGB image is resized to 128 by 128 before the DCT, a complete DCT coefficient set is exact for the 128 by 128 image, not for the original 2000 by 1100 samples. Conversely, exact original-resolution representation would require 6,600,000 RGB coefficients. The equations are finite and complete, but the resulting document may be thousands of pages long.

The system uses a typed DrawingModel as its intermediate representation. The graphical interface, command-line interface, renderer, metric calculation, and exporters operate on this common model. The principal exports are plain text, JSON, SVG, PNG, Markdown with LaTeX equations, LaTeX source, editable DOCX equations through Pandoc, and a typeset PDF through Tectonic, XeLaTeX, or pdfLaTeX.

Version 0.2.1 passed twelve automated tests in the supplied environment. It also repairs a platform-dependent OpenCV issue in which HoughLinesP may return arrays shaped as (N, 4), (N, 1, 4), or a single (4,) vector. The corrected normalizer converts these variants safely to four-coordinate segment tuples.

A code-level audit also identifies four implementation facts that are important for scientific interpretation:

  • the automatic mode selector chooses only between hybrid vector and DCT modes; Fourier mode is manual;
  • contour edges in the current hybrid pipeline are polygon edges encoded as degenerate cubic Bezier segments, rather than smooth cubic spline fits;
  • ellipse objects are supported by the data model, equation formatter, renderer, and SVG exporter, but the current detector does not create ellipses automatically;
  • DOCX and PDF generation depend on external converters. In version 0.2.1, missing converters may cause these files to be skipped while the always-available exports are still produced.

These points do not invalidate the mathematical model. They define precisely what the present implementation does and distinguish it from reasonable future extensions.

2. Problem formulation

2.1 Images as finite sampled functions

Let an image have width WW, height HH, and CC channels. The raster can be written as a discrete function

I:{0,…,W−1}×{0,…,H−1}×{0,…,C−1}→{0,…,255}.(1) I:\{0,\ldots,W-1\}\times\{0,\ldots,H-1\}\times \{0,\ldots,C-1\}\rightarrow \{0,\ldots,255\}. \qquad (1)

For an RGB image, C=3C=3. A grayscale image has C=1C=1. At this level, an image is neither mysterious nor intrinsically nonmathematical: it is a tensor with WHCWHC samples. The challenge is to replace those samples with a representation whose structure is useful to a person or another program.

A representation may be judged by several criteria:

  • reconstruction fidelity, measured against the raster;
  • compactness, often expressed by the number of primitives or coefficients;
  • interpretability, such as explicit lines, circles, or named frequency terms;
  • editability, meaning that a user can alter a geometric or spectral component;
  • stability, meaning that small image perturbations do not cause unacceptable model changes;
  • computational cost, both during fitting and during rendering.

These criteria conflict. A pixel-by-pixel basis is exact and stable but rarely concise. A small set of smooth curves is readable but cannot preserve photographic texture. A frequency basis is complete and mathematically regular but may obscure semantic parts of an object.

2.2 What “the equation of an image” can mean

The phrase can denote at least four different objects.

A geometric drawing equation describes visible boundaries and regions with parametric curves and primitive shapes. It is suitable for a diagram or logo.

A contour equation describes the boundary of a silhouette, often with a periodic parameter tt. It does not by itself encode interior texture.

A basis expansion expresses every sample in a chosen finite basis. A two-dimensional cosine series is one example. This is the natural interpretation for photographs.

A generative semantic model describes an image through objects, parts, materials, illumination, and scene geometry. That is a different research problem and is not claimed by the present project.

MathDraw Studio implements the first three meanings. It does not infer that a curve is a feather, an eye, a leaf, or a letter. In hybrid mode, text is traced as visible glyph geometry rather than recognized and retyped.

2.3 Taxonomy of exactness

Three notions should not be conflated.

  1. Model-exact reconstruction. The renderer evaluates the exported model without omitting any stored primitive or coefficient.
  2. Grid-exact reconstruction. A complete orthonormal DCT reproduces the selected discrete image grid to numerical precision.
  3. Source-exact reconstruction. The model reproduces the original file’s full raster dimensions, channel values, color interpretation, and any frame or page selection.

Hybrid vector and truncated Fourier models are generally approximations of source geometry. A full DCT is grid-exact. It is source-exact only if the selected equation grid and channel preparation preserve the source raster itself.

3. System architecture and data flow

The application is organized as a sequence of transformations. Input loading produces a normalized Pillow image. Optional resizing controls the computational scale. The selected mathematical mode then constructs a typed intermediate model. The same model is passed to an equation formatter, a renderer, metric calculation, and export adapters.

This separation is more than software housekeeping. It gives the project a clear mathematical contract:

image→ℱM→ℛÎ,(2) \text{image}\;\xrightarrow{\;\mathcal{F}\;}\;M \;\xrightarrow{\;\mathcal{R}\;}\;\widehat I, \qquad (2)

where ℱ\mathcal{F} is a mode-dependent fitting map, MM is a finite DrawingModel, and ℛ\mathcal{R} is the deterministic renderer. Equation export is another view of MM, not a second fitting process. Consequently, the equations, JSON, SVG, and preview image are intended to describe the same fitted object.

3.1 Typed intermediate representation

The model layer contains dataclasses for:

  • line segments;
  • circles;
  • ellipses;
  • cubic Bezier segments and paths;
  • Fourier coefficients and paths;
  • DCT coefficients and image models;
  • global image dimensions, coordinate-system metadata, mode, and processing metadata.

Typed storage avoids an unstructured formula dump. A line knows its endpoints; a Fourier term knows its integer frequency and complex coefficient; a DCT coefficient knows its channel and two frequency indices. This organization enables machine-readable JSON, deterministic rendering, grouped equations, and later conversion to other mathematical systems.

3.2 Mode selection

When the user selects Automatic, the image is resized to 128 by 128 and five low-cost characteristics are measured: white-pixel fraction, dark-pixel fraction, Canny edge density, mean HSV saturation, and a 32-bin grayscale entropy. Version 0.2.1 applies the following routing rule:

hybrid vector if{fwhite>0.35,s‾<0.18,fedge<0.30,otherwise DCT image.(3) \text{hybrid vector if} \begin{cases} f_{\mathrm{white}}>0.35,\\ \bar s<0.18,\\ f_{\mathrm{edge}}<0.30, \end{cases} \quad \text{otherwise DCT image}. \qquad (3)

Dark-pixel fraction and entropy are recorded but are not used in this decision. Fourier contour mode must be selected explicitly.

The rule should be read as an engineering heuristic, not as an image classifier. It is designed to route light-background, low-saturation, moderately sparse drawings toward vector processing. A colored technical diagram or a dark-background line drawing may be routed to DCT despite being geometrically simple. The GUI therefore retains manual mode selection.

4. Input handling and normalization

4.1 Supported file families

Common raster formats are opened through Pillow: PNG, JPEG, BMP, TIFF, WebP, the first frame of GIF, ICO, PPM, and PGM. Optional adapters add:

  • PDF page rasterization through PyMuPDF;
  • SVG rasterization through CairoSVG;
  • HEIC, HEIF, and AVIF through pillow-heif;
  • common camera RAW formats through rawpy.

The loader applies EXIF orientation before conversion to RGB. This is essential because camera files frequently store the physical pixel array in one orientation and request a display rotation through metadata. Fitting the untransposed raster would make coordinates inconsistent with the image seen by the user.

PDF and SVG are rasterized before analysis. Thus, the current application does not preserve original PDF vectors or import SVG path commands directly. A future native-vector importer could bypass edge detection and retain exact source paths.

4.2 Color normalization

All ordinary inputs are converted to RGB. Grayscale operations use OpenCV’s RGB-to-gray conversion, which forms a weighted luminance-like combination rather than a simple arithmetic mean. Let the converted value be denoted

Y(x,y)=wRR(x,y)+wGG(x,y)+wBB(x,y),(4) Y(x,y)=w_R R(x,y)+w_G G(x,y)+w_B B(x,y), \qquad (4)

with implementation-defined standard weights in OpenCV. The conversion reduces the data to a scalar field for edge, threshold, and contour operations. DCT mode may retain RGB channels or convert to one grayscale channel, depending on the configuration.

4.3 Resizing and the equation grid

Vector processing can restrict the longest image side to a user-selected maximum. The aspect ratio is preserved and Lanczos resampling is used. DCT processing similarly forms a thumbnail whose dimensions do not exceed the requested equation width and height and does not enlarge a smaller image.

Resizing changes the mathematical object being modeled. This is not merely a performance detail. If SS denotes the resampling operator, the model is fitted to S(I)S(I):

M=ℱ(S(I)).(5) M=\mathcal{F}(S(I)). \qquad (5)

A full DCT then reconstructs S(I)S(I) exactly, not necessarily II.

5. Coordinate systems

The internal model uses pixel coordinates with the origin at the upper-left. The xx coordinate increases to the right and yy increases downward. Equation export can transform points into two Cartesian alternatives.

For normalized coordinates,

X=xW−1,Y=1−yH−1.(6) X=\frac{x}{W-1},\qquad Y=1-\frac{y}{H-1}. \qquad (6)

Both axes lie in [0,1][0,1], provided W,H>1W,H>1, and YY increases upward.

For centered Cartesian coordinates, let

s=max(W,H)2.(7) s=\frac{\max(W,H)}{2}. \qquad (7)

Then

X=x−W/2s,Y=H/2−ys.(8) X=\frac{x-W/2}{s},\qquad Y=\frac{H/2-y}{s}. \qquad (8)

The longer dimension spans approximately [−1,1][-1,1]. The shorter dimension spans a narrower interval, preserving aspect ratio. This is preferable to independently scaling both axes to [−1,1][-1,1], which would distort circles into ellipses.

All control points and primitive parameters must be transformed consistently. For a circle, uniform centered scaling preserves circularity; normalized [0,1][0,1] scaling is anisotropic whenever W≠HW\ne H, so a pixel-space circle may require ellipse parameters in that coordinate system if strict geometry is to be preserved. The current formatter primarily transforms sampled/control coordinates and should therefore be interpreted in the chosen export convention.

6. Preprocessing and boundary evidence

The vector and Fourier pipelines begin from edge evidence. Version 0.2.1 combines two complementary boundary detectors: Canny edges and the morphological gradient of an Otsu-thresholded image.

6.1 Gaussian smoothing

Noise and compression artifacts can create unstable gradients. The grayscale image is first convolved with a Gaussian kernel when the blur parameter σ\sigma is positive:

Gσ(x,y)=12πσ2exp[−x2+y22σ2],Iσ=Gσ*Y.(9) G_\sigma(x,y)=\frac{1}{2\pi\sigma^2} \exp\!\left[-\frac{x^2+y^2}{2\sigma^2}\right], \qquad I_\sigma=G_\sigma * Y. \qquad (9)

The implemented default is σ=1.0\sigma=1.0. The kernel width is the nearest odd integer at least three and approximately 4σ4\sigma. Smoothing reduces high-frequency noise but also broadens narrow features. The user-visible Canny thresholds should therefore be interpreted jointly with the blur scale.

6.2 Canny edge detection

Canny formulated edge detection around detection probability, localization, and avoidance of multiple responses to a single edge [1]. In practical form, the method computes image gradients, suppresses nonmaximal responses across the gradient direction, and applies hysteresis thresholding. The application uses OpenCV’s Euclidean gradient magnitude (L2gradient=True) and defaults to lower and upper thresholds of 40 and 130.

If gxg_x and gyg_y are discrete derivatives, the magnitude is

∥∇Iσ∥2=gx2+gy2.(10) \|\nabla I_\sigma\|_2=\sqrt{g_x^2+g_y^2}. \qquad (10)

Pixels above the high threshold are accepted as strong edges. Pixels between thresholds are retained when connected to strong edges. This two-threshold procedure helps preserve weak continuations while rejecting isolated responses.

6.3 Otsu thresholding and morphological gradient

Otsu’s method selects a gray-level threshold by maximizing between-class variance, equivalently minimizing within-class variance for two histogram classes [2]. For class probabilities ω0(t),ω1(t)\omega_0(t),\omega_1(t) and means μ0(t),μ1(t)\mu_0(t),\mu_1(t), the objective is

σB2(t)=ω0(t)ω1(t)(μ0(t)−μ1(t))2.(11) \sigma_B^2(t)=\omega_0(t)\omega_1(t)(\mu_0(t)-\mu_1(t))^2.\qquad (11)

The implementation creates an inverse binary image and applies a 3 by 3 morphological gradient. If BB is a binary set and KK a structuring element, the gradient is

gradK(B)=(B⊕K)−(B⊖K),(12) \operatorname{grad}_K(B)=(B\oplus K)-(B\ominus K), \qquad (12)

where ⊕\oplus and ⊖\ominus denote dilation and erosion [9]. This boundary can recover high-contrast region outlines that the Canny thresholds might omit.

The Canny and threshold-gradient maps are combined by logical OR. A 3 by 3 morphological closing then fills small breaks:

B•K=(B⊕K)⊖K.(13) B\bullet K=(B\oplus K)\ominus K. \qquad (13)

Combining detectors increases recall but may create double boundaries or small spurious components. Subsequent contour filtering, primitive support tests, and complexity limits mitigate these effects.

6.4 Foreground mask and polarity

Hybrid vector mode also requires a filled foreground mask. The median intensity of the image border is used to infer whether the background is light or dark. An Otsu threshold is then constrained to avoid overly permissive masks:

  • for a light background, the threshold is clamped to at least 225 and at most 250, and darker pixels become foreground;
  • for a dark background, the threshold is clamped between 5 and 30, and brighter pixels become foreground.

A 2 by 2 closing repairs small mask gaps. The border-polarity assumption works well when the object does not occupy most of the frame boundary. It can fail for full-bleed artwork or photographs, which is one reason those inputs are better served by DCT mode.

7. Hybrid vector representation

Hybrid vector mode decomposes a drawing into explicit primitives and residual filled contours. The intended advantage is interpretability: a detected straight edge remains a line equation rather than hundreds of unrelated pixels.

7.1 Skeletonization

Line detection is applied to a one-pixel-wide approximation of the foreground. The project performs iterative morphological skeletonization with a cross-shaped structuring element. At iteration jj, the current binary set BjB_j is eroded and opened; the part removed by opening is accumulated:

Sj=Bj−(Bj∘K),Bj+1=Bj⊖K,(14) S_j=B_j-(B_j\circ K), \qquad B_{j+1}=B_j\ominus K, \qquad (14)

where ∘\circ denotes opening. The skeleton is the union of the residues SjS_j until the eroded set becomes empty. This construction preserves approximate medial structure while reducing thick strokes to narrow evidence for line fitting.

7.2 Stroke-width estimate

The Euclidean distance transform D(p)D(p) gives the distance from a foreground pixel to the nearest background pixel. On the skeleton, DD approximates the local stroke radius. The project estimates stroke width as

ŵ=2medianp∈SD(p),(15) \widehat w=2\,\operatorname{median}_{p\in S}D(p), \qquad (15)

clipped to the range 1 through 16 pixels. A median is used to reduce sensitivity to isolated thick regions. This estimate sets line-clustering tolerances and the width of the mask used to remove accepted primitives from residual contour processing.

7.3 Probabilistic Hough line detection

A line is represented in normal form as

xcosθ+ysinθ=ρ.(16) x\cos\theta+y\sin\theta=\rho. \qquad (16)

The normal representation avoids the singularity of slope-intercept form for vertical lines [4]. An image point (xi,yi)(x_i,y_i) votes for all parameter pairs satisfying

ρ(θ)=xicosθ+yisinθ.(17) \rho(\theta)=x_i\cos\theta+y_i\sin\theta. \qquad (17)

Collinear points generate sinusoids that intersect near a common accumulator location. The probabilistic variant uses a subset and returns finite line segments rather than infinite lines [5].

The implemented OpenCV call uses:

  • radial resolution of 1 pixel;
  • angular resolution π/360\pi/360;
  • vote threshold 25;
  • minimum segment length max(30,0.12min(W,H))\max(30,0.12\min(W,H));
  • maximum gap 10 pixels.

Candidate segments are not accepted blindly. The application samples evidence along each segment and requires an initial support fraction of at least 0.93. It groups segments whose angles differ by at most three degrees and whose normal offsets differ by at most max(2,ŵ)\max(2,\widehat w). Overlapping one-dimensional intervals on a common line are merged and revalidated at a support threshold of 0.90. At most 100 lines are retained.

This support-and-merge stage is important because Hough output often contains multiple nearby segments for one thick stroke. The process converts redundant detections into a smaller geometric set.

7.4 The v0.2.1 Hough-array correction

OpenCV bindings have returned probabilistic line segments in several array layouts, including (N,1,4), (N,4), and a single (4,) vector. Version 0.2.0 assumed that every row contained a nested iterable at row[0]. With an (N,4) array, row[0] is a scalar numpy.int32, causing the observed exception.

Version 0.2.1 converts the result to a NumPy array, checks that it can be arranged in groups of four, reshapes it to (-1,4), rejects malformed or nonfinite rows, and casts coordinates to integer tuples. The correction is a useful example of boundary validation: third-party library outputs should be normalized at the adapter boundary rather than allowed to leak shape assumptions into the mathematical code.

7.5 Circle detection

When enabled, circular structures are detected with OpenCV’s gradient Hough method after a median blur. The current defaults are:

  • inverse accumulator ratio dp=1.2;
  • minimum center distance min(W,H)/25\min(W,H)/25;
  • upper edge threshold 120;
  • center threshold 28;
  • minimum radius 3 pixels;
  • maximum radius min(W,H)/3\min(W,H)/3;
  • maximum 40 circles.

A circle with center (cx,cy)(c_x,c_y) and radius rr is exported parametrically as

x(t)=cx+rcost,y(t)=cy+rsint,0≤t<2π.(18) x(t)=c_x+r\cos t, \qquad y(t)=c_y+r\sin t, \qquad 0\le t<2\pi. \qquad (18)

Circle detection is disabled by default because repetitive ornament, text holes, and short arcs can produce false positives. It is most useful when large, well-defined circles are semantically important.

The model and exporters also support ellipses,

[x(t)y(t)]=[cxcy]+R(ϕ)[acostbsint],(19) \begin{bmatrix}x(t)\\y(t)\end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix}c_x\\c_y\end{bmatrix} + R(\phi) \begin{bmatrix}a\cos t\\b\sin t\end{bmatrix}, \qquad (19)

where R(ϕ)R(\phi) is a planar rotation. However, version 0.2.1 does not include an automatic ellipse detector.

7.6 Primitive subtraction

Accepted lines and circles are rasterized into a primitive mask. The line-mask width is approximately 1.8ŵ1.8\widehat w. This mask is removed from the foreground before contour extraction. The reason is representational economy: without subtraction, a straight stroke would be encoded twice, once as a line and again as two elongated contour boundaries.

Subtraction is necessarily approximate. If the mask is too narrow, residual fragments remain. If it is too wide, nearby curved details can be erased. The estimated stroke width provides an adaptive compromise, but dense illustrations may require disabling line detection or changing preprocessing settings.

7.7 Contour extraction and hierarchy

Residual foreground components are passed to findContours. Filled processing uses tree retrieval so that outer boundaries and nested holes are preserved. Candidate contours must contain at least twelve sampled points and satisfy an area filter. Parent regions are ordered before descendants; within comparable depth, larger regions are processed first.

For a binary image, a contour is an ordered sequence

P0,P1,…,Pn−1,Pi=(xi,yi).(20) P_0,P_1,\ldots,P_{n-1}, \qquad P_i=(x_i,y_i). \qquad (20)

Tree depth determines fill polarity in the current renderer: even-depth contours are filled black and odd-depth contours white. This reproduces holes by overpainting rather than by constructing one compound path with a formal winding rule. The result is effective for ordinary nested glyphs and regions, though extremely complex overlapping topology may be better represented by a true compound path.

7.8 Douglas-Peucker simplification

Dense contour chains are reduced with the Douglas-Peucker algorithm [3]. Given a polyline and tolerance ε\varepsilon, the method recursively retains endpoints and the intermediate point with greatest perpendicular distance when that distance exceeds ε\varepsilon. The resulting polyline remains within a prescribed geometric deviation under the algorithm’s distance criterion.

The implementation chooses

ε=max(0.25,min(0.8,0.004L)),(21) \varepsilon= \max\left(0.25, \min\left(0.8,0.004L\right)\right), \qquad (21)

where LL is contour arc length in pixels. If the simplified contour still exceeds the configured maximum vertex count, uniformly spaced indices are retained. The default maximum is 80 vertices per contour.

The first stage is geometry-aware; the second is a hard complexity cap. Aggressive caps can remove narrow corners or character detail. Increasing the vertex limit improves local fidelity at the cost of longer equation documents.

7.9 Cubic Bezier equations

A general cubic Bezier segment with control points P0,P1,P2,P3P_0,P_1,P_2,P_3 is

B(t)=(1−t)3P0+3(1−t)2tP1+3(1−t)t2P2+t3P3,0≤t≤1.(22) B(t)=(1-t)^3P_0+3(1-t)^2tP_1 +3(1-t)t^2P_2+t^3P_3, \quad 0\le t\le1. \qquad (22)

In coordinates,

x(t)=(1−t)3x0+3(1−t)2tx1+3(1−t)t2x2+t3x3.(23a) x(t)=(1-t)^3x_0+3(1-t)^2t x_1+3(1-t)t^2x_2+t^3x_3.\qquad (23\mathrm{a})

y(t)=(1−t)3y0+3(1−t)2ty1+3(1−t)t2y2+t3y3.(23b) y(t)=(1-t)^3y_0+3(1-t)^2t y_1+3(1-t)t^2y_2+t^3y_3.\qquad (23\mathrm{b})

Implementation note: polygon edges encoded as cubic segments

The delivered source contains spline utilities, including curve smoothing and Catmull-Rom-to-Bezier conversion, but the hybrid contour pipeline in version 0.2.1 does not call them. For each simplified polygon edge from P0P_0 to P3P_3, it places

P1=P0+P3−P03,P2=P0+2(P3−P0)3.(24) P_1=P_0+\frac{P_3-P_0}{3}, \qquad P_2=P_0+\frac{2(P_3-P_0)}{3}. \qquad (24)

Substitution into (22) gives

B(t)=(1−t)P0+tP3,(25) B(t)=(1-t)P_0+tP_3, \qquad (25)

so the cubic is exactly the straight segment between the two polygon vertices. The stored object is a valid cubic Bezier path, but it is not a smooth cubic fit to the original contour. The smoothing_passes configuration field is presently unused by this route.

This design has two merits: it preserves the simplified polygon exactly, and it uses one uniform path type for the renderer and exporters. Its limitation is visible angularity when the vertex cap is low. A future release can activate curvature-aware fitting while retaining the same data model.

7.10 Region rendering

Bezier paths are sampled at eight points per segment in the raster renderer. Closed filled contours are passed to OpenCV polygon filling; open paths are drawn as antialiased polylines. SVG export writes path commands directly. Because the current contour segments are straight cubics, eight samples are redundant geometrically but harmless.

8. Fourier contour representation

Fourier contour mode is appropriate when the principal information is a smooth closed outline. It represents geometry globally rather than as local segments.

8.1 Arc-length resampling

Raw contour samples are not generally spaced uniformly. Direct Fourier analysis of irregularly sampled points would entangle parameterization density with shape. The contour is therefore resampled to N=128N=128 points approximately uniform in cumulative arc length.

Let the cumulative distances be

s0=0,sj=∑i=1j∥Pi−Pi−1∥2.(26) s_0=0, \qquad s_j=\sum_{i=1}^{j}\|P_i-P_{i-1}\|_2. \qquad (26)

Interpolating at equally spaced values of ss produces samples Qn=(xn,yn)Q_n=(x_n,y_n) whose parameter more closely follows geometric distance.

8.2 Complex representation and DFT

The planar samples are combined into

zn=xn+iyn,n=0,…,N−1.(27) z_n=x_n+i y_n, \qquad n=0,\ldots,N-1. \qquad (27)

The discrete Fourier coefficients are

ck=1N∑n=0N−1znexp(−i2πknN).(28) c_k=\frac{1}{N}\sum_{n=0}^{N-1} z_n\exp\!\left(-i\frac{2\pi kn}{N}\right). \qquad (28)

A finite reconstruction for 0≤t<10\le t<1 is

ẑ(t)=∑k∈𝒦ckei2πkt.(29) \widehat z(t)=\sum_{k\in\mathcal K}c_k e^{i2\pi kt}.\qquad (29)

Writing ck=ak+ibkc_k=a_k+i b_k gives real coordinate equations:

x̂(t)=∑k∈𝒦(akcos2πkt−bksin2πkt).(30a) \widehat x(t)=\sum_{k\in\mathcal K}(a_k\cos 2\pi kt-b_k\sin 2\pi kt).\qquad (30\mathrm{a})

ŷ(t)=∑k∈𝒦(aksin2πkt+bkcos2πkt).(30b) \widehat y(t)=\sum_{k\in\mathcal K}(a_k\sin 2\pi kt+b_k\cos 2\pi kt).\qquad (30\mathrm{b})

Fourier descriptors have a long history in closed-curve analysis [6]. Their global nature makes them compact for smooth periodic shapes.

8.3 Harmonic selection

Version 0.2.1 retains the 2K+12K+1 frequencies with smallest absolute frequency around zero, where KK is the requested harmonic count and defaults to 18. It does not select the largest-magnitude coefficients. Low-frequency selection has a clear interpretation: global position and broad shape are represented before sharp local variation.

The zero-frequency coefficient is the complex centroid under the chosen sampling parameterization:

c0=1N∑n=0N−1zn.(31) c_0=\frac{1}{N}\sum_{n=0}^{N-1}z_n. \qquad (31)

Translation changes c0c_0 but not the nonzero coefficients. Scaling multiplies all coefficients; rotation multiplies them by a common unit complex factor. The present application exports raw coordinates rather than normalizing these transformations, because its purpose is reconstruction in the image frame rather than invariant classification.

8.4 Strengths and limitations

Fourier contours are smooth by construction. With few terms they suppress digitization noise and yield compact equations. Their main limitations are:

  • sharp corners require many harmonics and can exhibit ringing;
  • one series describes one closed contour, not a filled multicolor photograph;
  • local editing is nonlocal because changing one coefficient affects the entire curve;
  • starting point and traversal direction alter coefficient phases unless normalized;
  • self-intersections can arise under severe truncation.

The mode is therefore best for silhouettes, ornamental closed curves, and shape studies, not for arbitrary full-tone images.

9. Two-dimensional discrete cosine representation

The DCT mode is the mathematically complete route for photographs, textured objects, foods, animals in natural scenes, and images whose information is distributed across intensity and color rather than sparse boundaries.

9.1 One-dimensional orthonormal DCT

For a sequence f(x)f(x), x=0,…,W−1x=0,\ldots,W-1, the orthonormal DCT-II coefficient is

C(u)=α(u,W)∑x=0W−1f(x)cos[π(2x+1)u2W],(32) C(u)=\alpha(u,W) \sum_{x=0}^{W-1} f(x) \cos\left[\frac{\pi(2x+1)u}{2W}\right], \qquad (32)

where

α(u,W)={1/W,u=0,2/W,u>0.(33) \alpha(u,W)= \begin{cases} 1/\sqrt W,&u=0,\\ \sqrt{2/W},&u>0. \end{cases} \qquad (33)

The inverse has the same basis functions:

f(x)=∑u=0W−1C(u)α(u,W)cos[π(2x+1)u2W].(34) f(x)=\sum_{u=0}^{W-1}C(u)\alpha(u,W) \cos\left[\frac{\pi(2x+1)u}{2W}\right]. \qquad (34)

Ahmed, Natarajan, and Rao introduced the DCT as an efficient transform with strong energy-compaction properties for correlated signals [7].

9.2 Separable two-dimensional DCT

For channel cc of an HH by WW image, separability gives

Cc(v,u)=α(v,H)α(u,W)∑y=0H−1∑x=0W−1Ic(x,y)cos[π(2y+1)v2H]cos[π(2x+1)u2W].(35) C_c(v,u)=\alpha(v,H)\alpha(u,W) \sum_{y=0}^{H-1}\sum_{x=0}^{W-1}I_c(x,y) \cos\left[\frac{\pi(2y+1)v}{2H}\right] \cos\left[\frac{\pi(2x+1)u}{2W}\right]. \qquad (35)

The inverse equation exported by MathDraw Studio is

Ic(x,y)=∑v=0H−1∑u=0W−1Cc(v,u)α(v,H)α(u,W)cos[π(2y+1)v2H]cos[π(2x+1)u2W].(36) I_c(x,y)= \sum_{v=0}^{H-1}\sum_{u=0}^{W-1} C_c(v,u)\alpha(v,H)\alpha(u,W) \cos\left[\frac{\pi(2y+1)v}{2H}\right] \cos\left[\frac{\pi(2x+1)u}{2W}\right]. \qquad (36)

The implementation uses scipy.fft.dctn and idctn with norm="ortho". Under this normalization, the transform matrix is orthonormal and inverse reconstruction is numerically direct [12].

9.3 Why the full coefficient set is exact

Let AHA_H and AWA_W be orthonormal DCT matrices. A channel matrix II is transformed as

C=AHIAW𝖳.(37) C=A_H I A_W^{\mathsf T}. \qquad (37)

Because AH𝖳AH=IHA_H^{\mathsf T}A_H=I_H and AW𝖳AW=IWA_W^{\mathsf T}A_W=I_W,

AH𝖳CAW=AH𝖳AHIAW𝖳AW=I.(38) A_H^{\mathsf T} C A_W =A_H^{\mathsf T}A_H I A_W^{\mathsf T}A_W =I. \qquad (38)

Thus, in exact arithmetic, retaining all HWHW coefficients per channel reconstructs every sample exactly. Floating-point transforms may introduce errors on the order of machine precision. The renderer rounds the result and clips it to 8-bit range, so correctly reconstructed integer pixels normally recover their original values.

9.4 Coefficient truncation

In approximate mode, the application allocates approximately coefficient_count / C coefficients to each channel and retains the largest absolute values independently in each channel. If 𝒮c\mathcal S_c is the selected index set,

Îc(x,y)=∑(v,u)∈𝒮cCc(v,u)ϕv,u(x,y),(39) \widehat I_c(x,y)= \sum_{(v,u)\in\mathcal S_c} C_c(v,u)\,\phi_{v,u}(x,y), \qquad (39)

where ϕv,u\phi_{v,u} denotes the normalized cosine basis.

For an orthonormal basis, retaining the largest-magnitude coefficients minimizes squared reconstruction error among all subsets of the same cardinality. Parseval’s identity gives

∥Ic−Îc∥F2=∑(v,u)∉𝒮c|Cc(v,u)|2.(40) \|I_c-\widehat I_c\|_F^2 = \sum_{(v,u)\notin\mathcal S_c}|C_c(v,u)|^2. \qquad (40)

This provides a rigorous basis for magnitude selection. It differs from low-frequency rectangular truncation: a high-frequency coefficient is retained when its measured energy is large.

9.5 Color channels

For RGB images, three independent transforms are computed. The equation count is

Ncoeff=CWH.(41) N_{\mathrm{coeff}}=CWH. \qquad (41)

Representative exact RGB counts are:

Equation grid Coefficients
32 by 32 3,072
64 by 64 12,288
128 by 128 49,152
512 by 512 786,432
2000 by 1100 6,600,000

The coefficient list is complete but may be impractical as human reading material at high resolution. JSON or a binary scientific format is more appropriate for millions of values, while the document should present the defining equation and perhaps a structured appendix or machine-readable attachment.

9.6 Boundary behavior

Cosine basis functions correspond to an even extension of the sampled signal at the boundaries. This avoids the jump that a periodic Fourier extension may create between opposite image edges. The property contributes to the DCT’s energy compaction for many natural images, where intensity varies smoothly across neighboring pixels.

9.7 Exact DCT and file semantics

A DCT model does not automatically preserve:

  • ICC color profiles;
  • EXIF metadata;
  • alpha transparency;
  • animation frames beyond the first;
  • multiple PDF pages;
  • camera RAW sensor values before demosaicing;
  • JPEG compressed bitstream identity.

It preserves the normalized RGB or grayscale raster presented to the transform. “Exact” therefore refers to sample values in that mathematical domain, not byte-for-byte identity of the original container file.

10. Equation generation

Equation export traverses the DrawingModel and emits both a readable formula and all fitted numerical parameters.

10.1 Lines

For endpoints P0=(x0,y0)P_0=(x_0,y_0) and P1=(x1,y1)P_1=(x_1,y_1),

x(t)=x0+(x1−x0)t,0≤t≤1.(42a) x(t)=x_0+(x_1-x_0)t,\qquad 0\le t\le1.\qquad (42\mathrm{a})

y(t)=y0+(y1−y0)t,0≤t≤1.(42b) y(t)=y_0+(y_1-y_0)t,\qquad 0\le t\le1.\qquad (42\mathrm{b})

Parametric form handles vertical and horizontal segments uniformly and preserves finite extent.

10.2 Circles and ellipses

Circles use (18). Ellipses use (19) with semi-axes a,ba,b and rotation ϕ\phi. Parametric forms are preferable to implicit conics for rendering because they provide ordered points and a bounded parameter interval.

10.3 Bezier paths

Every stored segment is expanded into explicit x(t)x(t) and y(t)y(t) polynomials as in (23a)-(23b), with its numerical control coordinates. A multi-segment path is a piecewise parametric curve. If there are mm segments, it may be written compactly as

Γ(s)=Bj(s−j),j≤s≤j+1,j=0,…,m−1.(43) \Gamma(s)=B_j(s-j), \quad j\le s\le j+1, \quad j=0,\ldots,m-1. \qquad (43)

The document exporter generally lists segments separately because this is easier to inspect and edit in Word.

10.4 Fourier paths

The formatter lists each complex coefficient and expands the retained series into real coordinate equations (30). Frequencies can be negative, zero, or positive. A negative frequency is not redundant for a complex-valued contour in the same way it would be for a purely real one-dimensional signal.

10.5 DCT images

The formatter prints the defining inverse equation and every retained tuple

(c,v,u,Cc(v,u)).(44) (c,v,u,C_c(v,u)). \qquad (44)

The coefficient list is sufficient to reproduce the equation grid when accompanied by width, height, channel interpretation, normalization, and rounding convention.

11. Rendering and reconstruction

The renderer is an independent consumer of the model. This is important for validation: the displayed reconstruction is generated from stored primitives and coefficients, not from the original image.

11.1 Vector renderer

A white canvas is created. Lines, circles, and ellipses are rendered with OpenCV antialiasing. Bezier curves are sampled and rendered as polylines or filled polygons. Fourier paths are sampled at 600 parameter values and drawn as closed polylines.

Rasterization introduces its own approximation. A mathematically exact vector curve sampled at a finite number of points is rendered as a polyline approximation. SVG output preserves line, circle, and path geometry more directly and is the preferable vector interchange format.

11.2 DCT renderer

A dense coefficient array is reconstructed from the stored sparse list. The inverse orthonormal DCT is applied channel by channel. Values are rounded, clipped to [0,255][0,255], cast to 8-bit integers, and assembled as grayscale or RGB.

11.3 Representative demonstration

The supplied demonstration illustrates a central trade-off. The reconstruction preserves the dominant drawing structure, but its quality depends on line detection, foreground segmentation, contour simplification, and vertex limits. Hybrid mode is not intended to reproduce background texture or subtle color gradation. Those are DCT-mode responsibilities.

12. Quantitative diagnostics

The application resizes the reference image to the reconstruction dimensions and computes error metrics on corresponding samples.

For NN scalar channel samples,

MSE=1N∑i=1N(Ii−Îi)2,(45) \operatorname{MSE}=\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N}(I_i-\widehat I_i)^2, \qquad (45)

RMSE=MSE,(46) \operatorname{RMSE}=\sqrt{\operatorname{MSE}}, \qquad (46)

MAE=1N∑i=1N|Ii−Îi|.(47) \operatorname{MAE}=\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N}|I_i-\widehat I_i|. \qquad (47)

For 8-bit data, peak signal-to-noise ratio is

PSNR=20log10(255RMSE).(48) \operatorname{PSNR}=20\log_{10}\left(\frac{255}{\operatorname{RMSE}}\right). \qquad (48)

If RMSE is zero, PSNR is infinite.

These metrics measure pixel agreement, not perceptual or geometric correctness. A one-pixel translation of a sharp line may produce a large MSE despite being visually close. Conversely, a blurred approximation can have acceptable PSNR while losing corners important to a technical drawing. Recommended future metrics include contour Chamfer distance, Hausdorff distance, structural similarity, multiscale SSIM, and task-specific feature agreement.

13. Graphical user interface

The desktop application uses Tkinter and opens at approximately 1500 by 920 pixels. Its principal regions are:

  • input and reconstruction previews;
  • representation and coordinate controls;
  • vector preprocessing and complexity controls;
  • Fourier harmonic control;
  • DCT grid, coefficient, grayscale, and exactness controls;
  • equation and diagnostic views;
  • processing and export actions.

Image fitting runs in a single ThreadPoolExecutor worker so that the Tkinter event loop remains responsive. Completed work is returned to the main thread through after(). This is the correct threading discipline for Tkinter, whose widgets should not be updated directly from a worker thread.

The preview equation tab is truncated at 400,000 characters to protect interface responsiveness. Exported equations are not deliberately truncated. The GUI warns before very large exact DCT jobs, using 100,000 coefficients as a practical alert threshold.

14. Command-line interface

The command-line interface exposes the same processing pipeline and is preferable for reproducible experiments and batch use. Representative commands are:

mathdraw drawing.png \
  --mode hybrid_vector \
  --max-contours 250 \
  --bezier-samples 120 \
  --output output_vector
mathdraw silhouette.png \
  --mode fourier_contour \
  --harmonics 30 \
  --output output_fourier
mathdraw photo.jpg \
  --mode dct_image \
  --dct-width 160 \
  --dct-height 120 \
  --dct-coefficients 6000 \
  --output output_dct
mathdraw photo.jpg \
  --mode dct_image \
  --dct-width 64 \
  --dct-height 64 \
  --dct-exact \
  --output output_exact_64

For scientific use, the command, software version, dependency versions, input hash, output hash, and configuration should be stored together. The JSON metadata is a natural place for this provenance.

15. Export formats and document generation

15.1 Always-available exports

The base Python environment can create:

  • drawing_model.json;
  • equations.txt;
  • equations_full.md;
  • equations_full.tex;
  • reconstruction.png;
  • reconstruction.svg.

For DCT models, SVG contains an embedded raster reconstruction because millions of cosine terms are not naturally expressed as SVG geometry.

15.2 Editable DOCX equations

Pandoc converts Markdown/LaTeX mathematics into Office Math Markup Language (OMML) in a DOCX document [18]. The equations are native Word equation objects rather than screenshots. Users can select an equation and switch between professional and linear display.

DOCX generation requires a discoverable Pandoc executable. The project supports a system installation or pypandoc-binary. The most reliable Anaconda installation is:

conda install -c conda-forge pandoc

15.3 PDF generation

The LaTeX source is compiled by the first suitable engine found among Tectonic, XeLaTeX, and pdfLaTeX. PDF generation therefore requires one of those executables on PATH.

In version 0.2.1, the document exporter defaults to require_docx=False and require_pdf=False. Missing tools can therefore lead to a successful export popup that lists only Markdown and TeX, without DOCX or PDF. The absence of the filenames from the popup means they were not created. A future release should surface converter status before processing and provide an explicit partial-success message.

15.4 JSON as the canonical interchange record

Human-readable equations are valuable for inspection, but JSON is the safer complete record for large models. It preserves numeric values without typography conversion and can be validated against a schema. For large exact DCT models, a binary array container such as NumPy NPZ, HDF5, or Zarr would reduce size and loading time substantially.

16. Parameter interpretation and recommended use

16.1 Drawings and diagrams

Recommended starting point:

Parameter Typical value
Mode Hybrid vector
Maximum side 800 to 1200
Canny low 30 to 50
Canny high 100 to 150
Maximum contours 150 to 300
Maximum contour vertices 60 to 160
Straight-line detection enabled
Circle detection initially disabled
Coordinates centered Cartesian

Lower Canny thresholds increase recall but can introduce texture and compression edges. A larger contour limit preserves disconnected marks and text. A larger vertex limit preserves corners and curvature but lengthens the equation set.

16.2 Smooth silhouettes

Use Fourier contour mode. Begin with 12 to 24 harmonics. Increase the count when corners or small protrusions are important. Inspect for ringing and self-intersection. For classification rather than reconstruction, consider explicit normalization of translation, scale, rotation, starting point, and direction.

16.3 Photographs and dense patterns

Use DCT image mode. Choose the equation grid according to the intended output, not merely the input dimensions. A 64 by 64 or 128 by 128 grid is often suitable for a document demonstration. For a compact approximation, increase retained coefficients until PSNR and visual detail meet the task requirement. For exact grid reconstruction, retain every coefficient and prefer machine-readable output for large grids.

16.4 Text

Hybrid mode traces glyph boundaries. It preserves visible shape but does not identify characters, fonts, kerning, or text semantics. Small text may fragment under edge detection. An OCR-assisted extension could replace reliably recognized glyph contours with Unicode text plus font and layout metadata, while retaining contours for unrecognized decorative lettering.

17. Computational complexity and scaling

Let P=WHP=WH be the number of pixels, EE the number of edge pixels, QQ the total number of retained contour vertices, and KK the number of Fourier harmonics.

17.1 Preprocessing

Gaussian filtering, thresholding, morphology, distance transform, and ordinary image scans are approximately O(P)O(P) for fixed kernel sizes. Memory use is also O(P)O(P) for several intermediate arrays.

17.2 Hough processing

The classical Hough transform can be expensive because edge points vote across angle bins. Probabilistic segment detection reduces practical cost, but runtime remains sensitive to edge density and accumulator parameters. The support-validation stage is proportional to total sampled candidate length. Reducing false edges before Hough processing is often more effective than micro-optimizing the later code.

17.3 Contours and Bezier storage

Contour extraction is roughly linear in image size and boundary length. Douglas-Peucker complexity depends on geometry and implementation; worst-case behavior can be quadratic in the number of points, though typical contours are substantially cheaper. Stored segment count is O(Q)O(Q).

17.4 Fourier paths

For NN samples per contour, FFT coefficient calculation is O(NlogN)O(N\log N). Rendering a path at TT parameter values using 2K+12K+1 coefficients is O(TK)O(TK).

17.5 DCT

A separable fast DCT is approximately O(CHW(logH+logW))O(CHW(\log H+\log W)). Exact coefficient serialization is O(CHW)O(CHW) and can dominate runtime and file size. Formatting millions of coefficients into Word or PDF is far more expensive than computing the transform itself.

18. Verification and testing

The delivered version includes unit and integration tests for:

  • approximate DCT construction and reconstruction;
  • full-coefficient DCT exactness at the selected grid;
  • equation-document export behavior;
  • JSON, text, SVG, and PNG export;
  • Fourier-model creation;
  • end-to-end pipeline execution;
  • primitive detection and Hough-array normalization.

Running pytest -q in the supplied codebase produced:

............
12 passed

The tests execute under the available Python environment and the continuous-integration configuration targets Python 3.10, 3.11, and 3.12. Passing tests establish regression coverage for specified behaviors; they do not constitute a broad image-quality benchmark.

18.1 Recommended scientific validation suite

A stronger evaluation should use stratified datasets:

  • synthetic lines at varied angles and widths;
  • circles and arcs under noise and occlusion;
  • vector logos with known ground-truth paths;
  • handwriting and printed glyphs;
  • silhouettes with known parametric boundaries;
  • natural photographs across texture and color complexity;
  • high-frequency patterns and repeated ornament.

Metrics should include primitive precision/recall, endpoint error, radius error, contour distances, topology preservation, coefficient-rate versus distortion curves, runtime, peak memory, document size, and cross-platform export success.

19. Failure modes and troubleshooting

19.1 numpy.int32 object is not iterable

Cause: an OpenCV HoughLinesP result shaped (N,4) was processed as though each row were (1,4). Resolution: use the v0.2.1 primitive normalizer, which reshapes valid results to (-1,4).

19.2 DOCX or PDF absent after export

Cause: Pandoc or a LaTeX engine is not discoverable. Confirm with:

where pandoc
where tectonic
pandoc --version
tectonic --version

Install through conda-forge and relaunch the application from the activated environment. Existing Markdown and TeX files can be converted without reprocessing the image.

19.3 Too many noisy contours

Increase the lower Canny threshold, increase blur modestly, reduce maximum contours, or use DCT mode. Check whether the image has texture inconsistent with vector assumptions.

19.4 Missing thin strokes

Lower Canny thresholds, increase the maximum processing side, reduce blur, and increase contour count. JPEG artifacts may require a different balance between recall and noise.

19.5 Filled regions inverted or merged

The border-polarity rule may have inferred the wrong background. Crop or pad the image so that the border represents the true background, or choose a different mode. Full-bleed images are poor candidates for the current binary foreground model.

19.6 Angular curved boundaries

Increase the maximum contour vertices. The current hybrid implementation preserves simplified polygon edges as straight cubic segments. Smooth curvature requires Fourier mode or a future activated spline-fitting stage.

19.7 Excessively large equation documents

Reduce the DCT grid or coefficient count. Use JSON or a binary coefficient file for exact high-resolution storage. Word and PDF are presentation formats, not efficient numerical databases.

20. Limitations

The project is a useful mathematical conversion system, but its scope should be stated without exaggeration.

  1. No universal compact formula. Arbitrary images may require a coefficient count comparable to their pixel count.
  2. No semantic decomposition. Objects and parts are not recognized; equations describe geometry or samples.
  3. Rasterized vector inputs. SVG and PDF vector structure is not imported natively.
  4. Binary region model in hybrid mode. Rich color regions and gradients are not represented as vector paint models.
  5. Polygonal hybrid contours. Smooth spline fitting is not active in the current pipeline.
  6. Limited primitive family. Automatic detection covers lines and optional circles, not ellipses, arcs, rectangles, regular polygons, or repeated motifs as explicit objects.
  7. Heuristic mode selection. The automatic router is not trained or calibrated on a benchmark corpus.
  8. Pixel metrics only. The shipped diagnostics do not measure topology or perceptual structure.
  9. External document dependencies. DOCX and PDF depend on converters and are currently optional rather than enforced.
  10. Single frame/page defaults. Animation and multipage documents are not processed as sequences.

21. Research and engineering extensions

21.1 Curvature-aware spline fitting

Activate the existing Catmull-Rom and smoothing utilities or fit cubic Bezier segments by minimizing orthogonal distance subject to continuity constraints. For adjacent segments, C0C^0 continuity requires shared endpoints; C1C^1 continuity requires collinear tangent handles; C2C^2 continuity adds curvature constraints. Adaptive subdivision can allocate more segments near high curvature.

21.2 Expanded primitive inference

Add robust ellipse fitting, arc detection, rectangle and regular-polygon detection, and repeated-pattern discovery. Model selection could compare residual error plus a complexity penalty:

J(M)=D(I,ℛ(M))+λcomplexity(M).(49) J(M)=D(I,\mathcal R(M))+\lambda\,\operatorname{complexity}(M). \qquad (49)

This formalizes the preference for a small set of meaningful primitives when fidelity is comparable.

21.3 Color vectorization

Segment flat-color regions, estimate region adjacency, and assign fill and stroke colors. A layered vector model could combine primitives, paths, gradients, and alpha compositing. This would bridge the present black/white hybrid model and the full raster DCT model.

21.4 Wavelet and multiresolution bases

Wavelets provide localized spatial-frequency support and often represent sharp edges more efficiently than global cosine terms. A multiresolution mode could preserve coarse structure with scaling coefficients and local detail with sparse wavelet coefficients.

21.5 Semantic assistance without mathematical opacity

A segmentation or vision-language model could propose object masks, but the final representation should remain explicit and verifiable. Semantic labels should annotate geometric components rather than replace them with an opaque generative reconstruction.

21.6 Native vector import and symbolic export

SVG paths should be parsed directly and transformed into the common model without rasterization. Export adapters could target TikZ/PGF, Mathematica, MATLAB, GeoGebra, Desmos, and CAD interchange formats.

21.7 Scalable coefficient storage

For large exact DCT models, store coefficients in NPZ, HDF5, or Zarr with compression, chunking, checksums, and schema metadata. The Word/PDF report can include the defining equation, dimensions, normalization, coefficient statistics, and a reference to the attached machine-readable dataset.

21.8 Reproducibility and provenance

A production release should record:

  • input SHA-256;
  • software and dependency versions;
  • complete configuration;
  • selected image page/frame;
  • color conversion and resize operations;
  • coordinate convention;
  • model and output hashes;
  • test status.

This would make an exported equation model auditable and suitable for research workflows.

22. Installation and reproducible operation

22.1 Anaconda environment

From the project directory:

conda env create -f environment.yml
conda activate mathdraw-studio
python -m pip install -e .
python run_app.py

The environment file installs Python 3.11 and the principal numerical dependencies. Pandoc and Tectonic are included for document export.

22.2 Base Python dependencies

The project requires Python 3.10 or later and principally uses:

  • NumPy for arrays and numerical storage;
  • Pillow for raster I/O and resampling;
  • OpenCV for image processing and geometry detection;
  • SciPy for FFT and DCT operations;
  • Tkinter for the desktop interface.

Optional packages provide additional formats and documents.

22.3 Post-installation verification

Run:

python -m pytest -q
python run_app.py

For document export, also run:

pandoc --version
tectonic --version

A complete GUI export should list equations_full.docx and equations_full.pdf explicitly. Their omission indicates partial export.

23. Conclusion

MathDraw Studio rests on a straightforward but important principle: an image should be represented by mathematics appropriate to its structure. Sparse drawings benefit from explicit geometric primitives and paths. Closed silhouettes benefit from periodic Fourier representations. Photographs require a complete spatial basis such as the two-dimensional DCT. The project places these models behind one interface and one typed intermediate representation, allowing equations, reconstructions, and machine-readable exports to remain synchronized.

The strongest mathematical guarantee belongs to the full orthonormal DCT: all coefficients reconstruct the selected sample grid exactly, subject only to numerical arithmetic and output rounding. Hybrid and Fourier modes instead optimize interpretability and compactness and must be understood as approximations controlled by thresholds, contour limits, and harmonic count.

The present report also makes implementation boundaries explicit. Version 0.2.1 uses polygonal contour edges stored as cubic Bezier objects, routes automatic mode only between hybrid and DCT, does not yet detect ellipses, and relies on external tools for Word and PDF production. These are concrete, repairable engineering limits rather than conceptual defects. The architecture already provides clear extension points for smooth curve fitting, richer primitives, color vectorization, native vector import, multiresolution transforms, scalable coefficient storage, and stronger validation.

The result is not a claim that every image has a short elegant formula. It is a practical system for constructing a complete finite mathematical description at a chosen level of fidelity, while making the trade-off between readability, compactness, and exactness visible to the user.

Appendix A. Module-level responsibility map

preprocess.py grayscale, Canny/Otsu/morphology, foreground mask, auto mode
primitive.py skeletonization, stroke width, Hough lines/circles, normalization
contour.py contour hierarchy, simplification, path construction
geometry.py coordinate transforms, resampling, spline utilities
fourier.py contour resampling, FFT coefficients, retained harmonics
dct_image.py DCT construction, sparse/full coefficient selection, inverse DCT
models.py typed drawing-model dataclasses
pipeline.py orchestration of mode-dependent fitting
renderer.py model-to-raster reconstruction
equations.py plain-text mathematical equation generation
document_export.py Markdown, TeX, DOCX, and PDF production
exporters.py JSON, text, SVG, PNG, and document coordination
metrics.py MSE, RMSE, MAE, and PSNR
cli.py command-line configuration and execution
gui/main_window.py desktop controls, threading, previews, messages

Hough line theta step π/360\pi/360

Hough maximum gap 10 pixels

Maximum lines 100

Appendix C. Suggested acceptance criteria for a future release

A release intended for broad distribution should satisfy the following acceptance conditions.

  1. All supported file types either open correctly or produce an actionable dependency message.
  2. Automatic mode selection is tested against a labeled routing dataset.
  3. Every detected primitive has a confidence or support measure in JSON.
  4. Hybrid contours preserve holes and disconnected regions on a topology test suite.
  5. Full DCT reconstruction is pixel-identical at selected grids across supported platforms.
  6. DOCX and PDF dependency checks occur before export, with explicit partial-failure status.
  7. All output files include model version and input hash.
  8. GUI cancellation and large-job warnings are tested.
  9. Every release passes unit, integration, document-generation, and visual regression tests.
  10. Documentation is generated from or checked against code defaults to prevent drift.
